title: The butcher who taught a monk
hookLine: a monk burns two birds with a look, and a woman at a door tells him to wait
carry: svadharma: your own duty, done with care, is worship
tomorrow: seven hundred verses later, does Arjuna pick up his bow?
last: EACH IS GREAT IN ITS OWN PLACE.

lines: A MONK WHO BURNED TWO BIRDS.
cards: A young monk goes into the forest and meditates for years. He gets good at it. Maybe too good.

One day a crow and a crane start fighting in the branches above him, and dry leaves fall on his head. He looks up, furious, and a flash of fire leaves his eyes. The two birds fall to the ground, burned.
He's thrilled: I can burn birds with a look. Then he gets hungry, walks into town, and knocks on a door to beg for food. From inside, a woman calls out: wait a little, my son.
He's about to learn something the forest never taught him.

teach.b: Vivekananda tells this story in the Karma Yoga lecture called What Is Duty? The monk stands at the door, fuming. How dare she make me wait.
Doesn't she know what I can do? From inside, the woman says: don't think so much of yourself. There's no crow or crane here.
He's stunned. How did she know? When she finally comes out, she explains.

teach.h: SHE WAS CARING FOR HER HUSBAND.
teach.b: Her husband was ill, and she was caring for him. That was her duty, done with her whole heart, and it was all her practice. Through it, the story says, she had come to see more than his years in the forest had shown him.
Then she sends him on: go to the market and find the butcher. He'll teach you. The monk is shocked: a butcher, of all people, his teacher?
He goes anyway. The butcher, cutting meat, looks up: the lady sent you? Sit down, wait until I've finished.

teach.h: THE BUTCHER WHO FED HIS PARENTS FIRST.
teach.b: He takes the monk home, washes and feeds his old parents first, and only then sits down to teach him. What he teaches is a whole section of the Mahabharata, the Vyadha Gita, the song of the hunter-butcher.
Vivekananda's point is sharp. The woman and the butcher were not saints by job title.
Each did their svadharma, their own duty, the one in front of them, without selfishness and with care.

teach.h: DONE WITH CARE, IT IS WORSHIP.
teach.b: Work done like that, he says, is worship. Fire from the eyes is not the goal.

how: Many Hindus understand caring for parents, spouse and children as dharma and as a form of worship, and the Vyadha Gita, the butcher's teaching in the Mahabharata, is often cited to show that holiness isn't tied to a particular job.

o: a long illness that keeps someone in bed for years
a forest hermit who has given up the world entirely
a hunter or butcher, like the one who taught the monk

games.q: who did what — tap the pairs.
p: burned a crow and a crane

s: in the story, the monk's years of meditation made him wiser than the woman
she knew his thoughts through a door. her practice was caring for her husband.
the butcher's teaching is part of the Mahabharata
it's called the Vyadha Gita, the song of the hunter-butcher.
Vivekananda uses the story to say some jobs can't be holy
his point is the opposite: any duty, done with care and without selfishness, is worship.

games.q: the monk thinks his years in the forest make him holier than a wife at a sickbed and a butcher at his counter. what does the story teach?
o: he's right: holiness needs a forest.
your own duty, done with care and without selfishness, is worship.
only a priest's work can be holy.
games.why: the woman and the butcher saw further than the monk. svadharma, done with care, was their practice.

practice: Bring to mind whoever made you wait most recently, the pharmacy line, a kid who needed one more thing, a parent on the phone, and notice the flash of heat without pushing it away.
Then picture the woman at the door, doing what was in front of her. Breathe in and let the waiting be part of the work; breathe out and let the heat cool.

wordCard.voice: Vyadha, a hunter, here the butcher who taught the monk. His svadharma, done without selfishness and with care, was already his practice.

orig.note: Sanskrit: vyadha, a hunter; in this story the dharma-vyadha, the righteous hunter-butcher of the Mahabharata.

carryVoice: Your line: svadharma: your own duty, done with care, is worship. Whoever keeps you waiting might be caring for someone. Day two hundred sixty-three, complete.

sources.ref: Swami Vivekananda, Karma Yoga (1896), ch. 4, 'What Is Duty?' (the monk, the woman and the butcher)
Mahabharata, Vana Parva (Markandeya's tales: the devoted wife and the dharma-vyadha of Mithila)
Bhagavad Gita 3.35 (svadharma: better one's own dharma, imperfectly done)
